demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'Feels Present Not Past' and 'Full Sensory Reliving' indicate highly intrusive, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' These can sometimes coexist, but stated this strongly they pull in opposite directions and are hard to reconcile as the same memory profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The Threat items depict pervasive fear of being physically attacked by other people ('watch other people closely', 'back to wall', 'stay alert at night'), which does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma, threat is more plausibly guilt, condemnation, or fear of consequences, not generalized interpersonal danger.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Mirror Checking' is not well linked to the rest of the profile. Nothing in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Negative Appraisals suggests appearance-focused concern, dissociation needing visual reassurance, or checking for injury; as selected, it appears clinically disconnected.

Mirror checking is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; it more strongly suggests concerns about visible injury, appearance, or being followed, none of which are supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Back-to-wall hypervigilance and scanning the room imply an interpersonal or attack-related threat context. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which centers on guilt, reliving, and self-blame after accidentally injuring someone rather than danger from other people.

vignette: Michael, a 34-year-old school counselor and married father of two, was driving home from a faculty meeting when a sudden brake failure sent his car into a parked SUV. The impact tore a hole in the front of the SUV, and a passenger-a college student-was pinned beneath the seat, unable to move. The sheer intensity of that moment left a constant itch of stress whenever he felt the hum of a car engine or the distant rumble of a commuter train, each sound dredging up the image of the student's limp body and his own sudden, helpless hands. Each time the memory flared, he could not shake the feeling that the accident was still happening; the phantom blood and the echo of screams sharpened his awareness, forcing him to stay alert even when he was alone in his office. His heightened vigilance pushed him to occupy his mind constantly-he began filling conference rooms with lesson plans, rehearsing counseling scripts, and scrolling through school newsletters to keep his thoughts away from the unrelenting phantom scene. Even the thought of a routine medical examination, with its sterile smell and humming equipment, flooded him with the same rush of fear he felt during the accident, pulling the vivid memory back into his awareness. Each burst of intrusive imagery sharpened Michael's sense of personal failure; he could not stop questioning whether his distraction had let the student suffer, and the doubt that flooded him spiraled into self-blame, as if he were the cause of the tragedy. He also deliberately avoided thinking about the accident, filling his mind instead with lesson plans. That self-blame, in turn, became a cue for distraction; he pushed even harder to keep his mind occupied, hoping the mental noise would drown out the shame he felt about his own perceived incompetence. His growing conviction that he had ruined everything for the student heightened his sensitivity to any sign of danger, turning ordinary traffic sounds into potential sirens of doom, and making him hyper-alert to every new event that might remind him of the crash. He doubted his own judgment and feared he could never protect anyone again. Stressful triggers also set off a distinct avoidance pattern: Michael found himself steering clear of any interaction with law-enforcement officers, who appeared at school during safety drills or in the hallway after a student's report of vandalism; each encounter forced him to engage in mental distraction. Whenever he heard the wail of a police siren, he could not shake the thought that the officers were the same people who might have saved the student, and the resulting shame fed back into his negative self-appraisal. Each sensory flash of the accident-the metallic tang of crushed metal, the muffled scent of broken plastic-reminded him that he could never undo what happened, reinforcing the belief that his life was irreparably destroyed. The smell of exhaust in a crowded hallway, the sudden flicker of headlights on a rainy night, and the echo of a footstep on a wooden floor all became instant triggers that ripped the memory out of storage and into his present consciousness. That state of constant alertness kept his brain primed for danger, so when a mundane classroom door creaked, his mind automatically linked it to the creaking of the damaged SUV frame, pulling the vivid accident back into view. However, the mental gymnastics that kept him distracted also reinforced his need to stay on guard; the more he avoided the raw emotion, the deeper his sense of vulnerability grew, creating a vicious cycle of vigilance and avoidance. Because he routinely avoided police and other stressful cues, he found himself caught in a loop where each avoidance event led to a new trigger-when he finally confronted a cop at a school event, the anticipation alone flooded him with the same racing heart he felt during the crash. Michael's escalating cycle of intrusive memories, self-doubt, and avoidance had eroded his sense of safety, leaving him exhausted and isolated at work and home. The turning point came when a sudden panic attack during a parent-teacher conference forced him to seek therapy, hoping to break the loop and reclaim his life.
